claims.claim: Modernity has traditionally been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the natural environment through a process of de-naturalization, a view questioned by Hannah Arendt who argues instead that re-naturalization has taken place to the detriment of the human world.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modernity, in philosophical and sociological literature, has “traditionally” been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment. The process of modernization, from this point of view, is the process of de-naturalization . This widely shared conviction has basically been questioned by Hannah Arendt. During the centuries of modern age, in the detriment of the commonly created and uphold human world, process of re-naturalization has been taking place, Arendt argues.

claims.claim: In The Human Condition, the problem of the relation between the natural and artificial is inserted into two narratives—cultural criticism and political philosophy—which introduce ambivalences and inconsistencies into Arendt's argumentation.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The problem of the relation of natural and artificial, in The Human Condition (1958), has been inserted in two narratives; one of them is the narrative of cultural criticism and another is that of political philosophy. These narratives have been embedded in different contexts borrowing ambivalences and inconsistencies to Arendt’s argumentation.

definitions.definition: The process of modernization viewed as the supplanting of nature by artifacts and the destruction of the originally given natural environment.
A process taking place during the modern age, enhanced by technology, to the detriment of the commonly created and upheld human world.

distinctions.distinction: The Arendtian critique of modernity takes a difference between the notions of Earth and world.

must_not_be_lost: Arendt transformed the inherited dichotomy of natural and artificial from German cultural criticism by incorporating Heideggerian philosophy within the context of a political philosophy based on plurality.
unresolved_context: Specific details regarding the complete influence of Martin Heidegger's philosophy and the distinct impact of the American intellectual climate on Arendt's later formulations beyond general mention.
